strategy.why_this_method: Eigenvalues are exactly the roots of $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. For a $2\times2$ matrix the determinant is a quadratic in $\lambda$, which is quick to solve.
strategy.alternatives: For a $2\times2$ matrix you can also use trace and determinant: the eigenvalues sum to the trace (4) and multiply to the determinant (3).

steps.title: Set up the characteristic equation
steps.explanation: A number $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue when $A-\lambda I$ is not invertible, which happens exactly when its determinant is zero. Subtract $\lambda$ from the diagonal entries only.
steps.common_mistake: Subtracting $\lambda$ from every entry instead of only the diagonal.

steps.title: Expand the determinant
steps.explanation: For $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ the determinant is $ad-bc$. Expanding $(2-\lambda)^2$ gives $4-4\lambda+\lambda^2$.

steps.title: Factor the characteristic polynomial
steps.explanation: Two numbers that multiply to 3 and add to $-4$ are $-1$ and $-3$.

steps.title: Read off the eigenvalues
steps.explanation: Each factor gives one eigenvalue. As a check, they add to the trace $2+2=4$ and multiply to the determinant $4-1=3$.

final_answer.domain_notes: The matrix is symmetric, so both eigenvalues are real.

check.detail: Sum $1+3=4$ equals the trace and product $1\cdot3=3$ equals the determinant.

hints: Which equation do all eigenvalues of a matrix satisfy?
Write $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ by subtracting $\lambda$ on the diagonal.
